source_text: Ταῦτ᾿ ἐστὶν ἃ λέγουσι καὶ τοιούτοις παραπλήσια ἐν ἀπείροις συγγράμμασι· πείθουσι δὲ ἐντυγχάνειν τῷ περὶ κράσεως καὶ μίξεως λόγῳ τοὺς μαθητευομένους, ὃς μεμελέτηται πολλοῖς, ἀλλὰ καὶ Ἀνδρονίκῳ τῷ περιπατητικῷ. Λέγουσιν οὖν οἱ Σηθιανοὶ τὸν περὶ κράσεως καὶ μίξεως λόγον συνεστάναι τῷδε τῷ τρόπῳ· τὴν ἀκτῖνα τὴν φωτεινὴν ἄνωθεν ἐγκεκρᾶσθαι, καὶ τὸν σπινθῆρα τὸν ἐλάχιστον ἐν τοῖς σκοτεινοῖς ὕδασι κάτω καταμεμῖχθαι λεπτῶς καὶ συνηνῶσθαι καὶ γεγονέναι ἐν ἑνὶ φυράματι, ὡς μίαν ὀσμὴν ἐκ πολλῶν καταμεμιγμένων ἐπὶ τοῦ πυρὸς θυμιαμάτων, καὶ δεῖ τὸν ἐπιστήμονα, τῆς ὀσφρήσεως ἔχοντα κριτήριον εὐαγές, ἀπὸ τῆς μιᾶς τοῦ θυμιάματος ὀσμῆς διακρίνειν λεπτῶς ἕκαστον τῶν καταμεμιγμένων ἐπὶ τοῦ πυρὸς θυμιαμάτων, οἱονεὶ στύρακα καὶ σμύρναν καὶ λίβανον, ἢ εἴ τι ἄλλο εἴη μεμιγμένον. Χρῶνται δὲ καὶ ἑτέροις παραδείγμασι, λέγοντες καταμεμῖχθαι καὶ χρυσίῳ χαλκόν, καὶ τέχνη τις εὕρηται ἡ διακρίνουσα τὸν χαλκὸν ἀπὸ τοῦ χρυσίου. Ὁμοίως δὲ κἂν ἐν ἀργύρῳ κασσίτερος ἢ χαλκὸς ἤ τι τῶν ὁμογενῶν καταμεμιγμένον εὑρεθῇ, μίξεως τινὶ τέχνῃ κρείττονι καὶ ταῦτα διακρίνεται. Ἤδη δέ τις καὶ ὕδωρ μεμιγμένον οἴνῳ διακρίνει. Οὕτω, φασί, κἂν πάντα τὰ συγκεκραμένα διακρίνεται. Καὶ δὴ ἀπὸ τῶν ζῴων, φησί, καταμάνθανε. Τελευτήσαντος γὰρ τοῦ ζῴου ἕκαστα διακρίνεται, καὶ λυθέντος οὕτω τὸ ζῷον ἀφανίζεται. Τοῦτο ἐστὶ, φησί, τὸ εἰρημένον· Οὐκ ἦλθον εἰρήνην βαλεῖν ἐπὶ τὴν γῆν, ἀλλὰ μάχαιραν, τουτέστι τὸ διχάσαι καὶ χωρίσαι τὰ συγκεκραμένα. Διχάζεται γὰρ καὶ διακρίνεται ἕκαστα τῶν συγκεκραμένων οἰκείου χωρίου τυχόντα. Ὡς γάρ ἐστι χωρίον συγκράσεως τοῖς ζῴοις ἅπασιν ἔν, οὕτω καὶ τῆς διακρίσεως καθέστηκεν ἕν, ὃ οἶδεν οὐδείς, φησίν, ἧ μόνοι ἡμεῖς, οἱ ἀναγεννώμενοι πνευματικοὶ οὐ σαρκικοί, ὧν ἔστι τὸ πολίτευμα ἐν οὐρανοῖς ἄνω. Οὕτω παρεισδύοντες διαφθείρουσι τοὺς ἀκροωμένους, ὁτὲ μὲν ἀποχρώμενοι ῥητοῖς, εἰς ὃ θέλουσι συνάγοντες κακῶς τὰ καλῶς εἰρημένα, φωλεύουσί τε τὸ ἑαυτῶν ἀδίκημα διὰ παραβολῶν ὧν βούλονται. Πάντα οὖν, φησί, καθὼς εἴρηται, τὰ συγκεκραμένα ἔχει χωρίον ἴδιον καὶ τρέχει πρὸς τὰ οἰκεῖα, ὡς σίδηρος πρὸς τὴν ἡρακλείαν λίθον, καὶ τὸ ἄχυρον ἠλέκτρου πλησίον, καὶ τῷ κέντρῳ τοῦ θαλασσίου ἱέρακος τὸ χρυσίον. Οὕτως ἡ τοῦ καταμεμιγμένου τῷ ὕδατι φωτὸς ἀκτίς, οἰκείου χωρίου ἐκ διδασκαλίας καὶ μαθήσεως μεταλαβοῦσα, σπεύδει πρὸς τὸν λόγον τὸν ἄνωθεν ἐλθόντα ἐν εἰκόνι δουλικῇ, καὶ γίνεται μετὰ τοῦ λόγου λόγος ἐκεῖ, ὅπου λόγος ἐστί, μᾶλλον ἢ ὁ σίδηρος πρὸς τὴν ἡρακλείαν λίθον. Καὶ ὅτι ταῦθ᾿ οὕτως ἔχει, φησί, καὶ πάντα διακρίνεται ἐπὶ τῶν οἰκείων τόπων τὰ συγκεκραμένα, μάνθανε. Φρέαρ ἐστὶν ἐν Πέρσαις ἐν Ἄμπῃ πόλει παρὰ τὸν Τίγριν ποταμόν· ᾠκοδόμηται δὲ παρὰ τὸ φρέαρ ἄνω δεξαμενή τις ἔχουσα τρεῖς ἀφετηρίας ἀπ᾿ αὐτῆς. Οὗ φρέατος ἀντλήσας κάδδῳ ἀνενέγκας τὸ ἀπὸ τοῦ φρέατος ἀντληθὲν ὅ τι ποτέ ἐστιν, ἔχεεν εἰς τὴν παρακειμένην δεξαμενήν· τὸ δὲ χυθὲν ἐλθὸν ἐπὶ τὰς ἀφετηρίας ἐν ἑνὶ σκεύει ἀναληφθὲν διακρίνεται. Καὶ ἐν μὲν πρώτῃ ἄλας πηγνύμενον δείκνυται, ἐν ἑτέρᾳ δὲ τῶν ἀφετηριῶν ἄσφαλτος, ἐν δὲ τῇ τρίτῃ ἔλαιον. Μέλαν δέ ἐστι τὸ ἔλαιον, ὡς, φησί, καὶ Ἡρόδοτος ἱστορεῖ, καὶ ὀσμὴν παρεχόμενον βαρεῖαν· ῥαδινάκην δὲ αὐτὸ οἱ Πέρσαι καλοῦσιν. Ἤρκει, φασὶν οἱ Σηθιανοί, πρὸς ἀπόδειξιν τοῦ προκειμένου ἡ τοῦ φρέατος ὁμοιότης πάντων μᾶλλον τῶν προειρημένων.
pass_a_gloss: These things are what they say and similar things in countless writings; they persuade the disciples to examine the concept of mixture and separation, which has been studied by many, but also by Andronicus the Peripatetic. The Sethians say, then, that the concept of mixture and separation is composed in the following way: the bright ray is mixed from above, and the smallest spark is subtly mixed and united with the dark waters below, and has become one mixture, just as one scent from many mixed incense sticks on the fire, and it is necessary for the knowledgeable person, having a clear criterion of smell, to distinguish each of the mixed incense sticks on the fire, such as styrax and myrrh and frankincense, or whatever else is mixed. They also use other examples, saying that bronze is mixed with gold, and a technique has been discovered that distinguishes bronze from gold. Similarly, even if tin or bronze or something of the same kind is found mixed with silver, it is distinguished by a superior technique of mixture. Already someone can distinguish water mixed with wine. Thus, they say, all mixed things can be distinguished. And from animals, he says, learn: when an animal dies, each part is distinguished, and when the animal is dissolved, it disappears. This, he says, is what was said: I did not come to bring peace on earth, but a sword, that is, to separate and distinguish the mixed things. For each of the mixed things is separated and distinguished, having fallen into its own region. Just as there is a region of mixture for all animals, so also there is one region of separation, which no one knows, he says, except us, the spiritual reborn, not fleshly, whose citizenship is in heaven above. Thus, sneaking in, they corrupt the listeners, sometimes using speeches to gather evilly the well-spoken things, and they hide their own injustice through parables of their choice. All things, then, as has been said, have their own region and run to their own things, like iron to the Heraclean stone, and chaff to the side of amber, and gold to the center of the sea-hawk. Thus the ray of light mixed with water, having received its own region through teaching and learning, hastens to the Word that came from above in a servile image, and becomes Word with the Word there, where Word is, rather than iron to the Heraclean stone. And that these things are so, he says, and all mixed things are distinguished in their own places, learn. There is a well in Persia in the city of Ambe near the Tigris river; and a cistern has been built above the well, having three outlets from it. When someone draws from the well with a bucket and brings up what is drawn from the well, whatever it is, and pours it into the nearby cistern, what is poured comes to the outlets and is taken up in one vessel and distinguished. And in the first outlet, salt is shown, in the second outlet, asphalt, and in the third outlet, oil. The oil is black, as Herodotus also tells, and has a heavy scent; the Persians call it rhadinake. The Sethians say that the similarity of the well is sufficient proof of the proposed thing, rather than all the previously mentioned things.

pass_b_english: This is what they say, along with similar claims in countless writings. They persuade their disciples to investigate the theory of mixture and separation—a theory studied by many, including Andronicus the Peripatetic. The Sethians maintain that this theory works as follows: a bright ray is mixed in from above, while the tiniest spark is subtly blended and joined with the dark waters below, forming a single mixture. They compare it to a single fragrance rising from many incense ingredients—styrax, myrrh, frankincense, or whatever else—blended together on the fire. They insist that an expert, possessing a keen sense of smell, can distinguish each individual ingredient from that one combined scent. They offer other illustrations as well: gold mixed with bronze, yet a technique exists to separate the bronze from the gold. Likewise, if tin or bronze or any similar metal is found alloyed with silver, a superior refining method can distinguish them. Even water mixed with wine can be separated, they say. So, they claim, every mixed substance can be resolved into its components.

And, he says, learn from living creatures: when an animal dies, each part separates out, and when the body dissolves, the creature ceases to be. This, he says, is the meaning of the saying: "I did not come to bring peace on earth, but a sword" (Matthew 10:34)—that is, to divide and separate what has been mixed together. For each of the mixed elements is divided and distinguished, finding its own proper region. Just as there is a single region of mixture for all living things, so there is also a single region of separation, which no one knows, he says, except us—the spiritually reborn, not fleshly—whose citizenship is in the heavens above. By slipping in this way, they corrupt their listeners, sometimes using set speeches to twist well-spoken truths toward their own evil ends, and they conceal their own injustice behind parables of their own choosing.

All things, then, as has been said, possess their own proper region and rush toward it—like iron to the Heraclean lodestone, chaff to amber, and gold to the center of the sea-hawk. In the same way, the ray of light mixed with water, having received its proper region through instruction and learning, hastens to the Word that came from above in a servant's form, and becomes Word with the Word there, where the Word is—more strongly than iron draws to the Heraclean stone. And that matters stand thus, he says, and that all mixed things are separated each to its own place—learn this. There is a well in Persia, in the city of Ambe beside the Tigris River. Above it a cistern has been built with three outlets. When someone draws water from the well with a bucket and pours whatever comes up into the adjacent cistern, the liquid reaches the outlets, is collected in a single vessel, and separates. At the first outlet salt appears, at the second asphalt, at the third oil. The oil is black, as Herodotus also records, and gives off a heavy scent; the Persians call it rhadinake. The Sethians say that the likeness of this well alone proves their point more convincingly than all the previous examples.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the complex theological and scientific analogies used by the Sethians as described by Hippolytus. Pass A preserves the nuances of the Greek, and Pass B provides a fluent rendering that maintains the meaning of Pass A and the source. The scripture citation (Matthew 10:34) is correctly identified and added to the English text.
